nuristani_bagisht.name: makes the irrigation channels run and the flood-fed fields prosper
nuristani_bagisht.notes: River and wealth god; the prosperity of the flood-watered terraces of the Bashgal valley was attributed to him.

sources.reference: Robertson, The Kafirs of the Hindu-Kush (1896)

phoenician_astarte.name: shines as the evening star (Venus) and governs the heavens
phoenician_astarte.notes: Identified with the planet Venus; depicted with a star within a circle.

sources.reference: Bonnet, Astarte: dossier documentaire et perspectives historiques (1996)

ovambo_kalunga.name: sends the rain and provides for the created world
ovambo_kalunga.notes: As supreme creator and provider of rain, approached through royal ancestors who act as intermediaries.

sources.reference: Aarni, The Kalunga Concept in Ovambo Religion from 1870 Onwards (1982)

ossetian_satana.name: brews the first beer of the Narts
ossetian_satana.notes: After seeing a bird faint from eating wild hops, Satana mixed the hops with ground malt and so invented Ossetian beer (bægæny), the drink of the Nart feasts.

sources.reference: Dumézil, Le livre des héros: Légendes sur les Nartes (1965)

palauan_uchelianged.name: commands land to rise from the barren sea and sets the heavens in order
palauan_uchelianged.notes: The sky high-god who, gazing on the empty waters, ordered the islands to emerge and ranked the cosmos after Latmikaik's brood raised the firmament.

sources.reference: Parmentier, The Sacred Remains: Myth, History, and Polity in Belau (1987)

otomi_zithu.name: rules the band of nocturnal earth-demons
otomi_zithu.notes: Lord of the zithü (devils/demons); enthroned at the apex of the night-pantheon and merged in some tellings with the lunar figure, he commands the malevolent powers of the underworld.

sources.reference: Galinier, La mitad del mundo: cuerpo y cosmos en los rituales otomíes (1990)
Lipiński, Dieux et déesses de l'univers phénicien et punique (1995)

sources.reference: Murie & Dorsey, Ceremonies of the Pawnee (1981)

nupe_soko.name: the Ketsa rock offering against flood
nupe_soko.cadence: in times of danger of flood
nupe_soko.notes: A white cow, white fowl (cork) and honey were sacrificed at the foot of a rock called Ketsa; Nadel records the Etsu of Patigi sending a fowl in 1936 for the peace and prosperity of the kingdom.

sources.reference: Nadel, Nupe Religion (1954)

nuristani_imra.name: goat sacrifice and juniper bonfire at the temple of Imra
nuristani_imra.cadence: seasonal and on request of pilgrims
nuristani_imra.notes: The cult centred on the sacrifice of goats and on purifying bonfires whose juniper smoke mixed with burnt blood and butterfat; the great temple of Imra drew regional pilgrims.

sources.reference: Robertson, The Kafirs of the Hindu-Kush (1896)

nuristani_gish.name: war-rites and victory offerings at the shrine of Gish
nuristani_gish.notes: The most active cult among the Siah-Posh Kafirs of the Bashgal valley; Gish was invoked for victory and clan protection, with sacrifices and dances at his shrine and effigy.

sources.reference: Robertson, The Kafirs of the Hindu-Kush (1896)

nuristani_disani.name: birth offerings at the shrine of Disani
nuristani_disani.cadence: at the birth of a son and at agricultural feasts
nuristani_disani.notes: Men presented a goat to Disani at the birth of each son; as great mother-goddess she oversaw all births and the fertility of fields and herds, her carved effigy housed in a small shrine.

sources.reference: Robertson, The Kafirs of the Hindu-Kush (1896)

obatala.name: Obatala festival (white-cloth feast)
obatala.notes: Worshippers process in white cloth and beads, offer boneless animals (especially the giant snail, igbin), white chalk (efun), coconut and snail water; palm wine is strictly forbidden in his worship.

sources.reference: Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief (1962)

ogun.name: Ogun festival (Odun Ogun)
ogun.notes: Smiths donate new cutlasses, hoes and gongs; the shrine is dressed with palm fronds, cowries and kola, and a dog (Ogun's sacred animal) is sacrificed. Oaths are sworn by kissing iron in his name.

sources.reference: Barnes (ed.), Africa's Ogun: Old World and New (1997)

oshun.name: Osun-Osogbo festival
oshun.notes: A pilgrimage and procession to the Osun River and its sacred grove at Osogbo, led by the Arugba (votary bearing the sacrifice-calabash); offerings of honey and brass at the river renew the covenant between the goddess and the town.

sources.reference: UNESCO World Heritage nomination, Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove (2005); Murray, Beier

olokun.name: Olokun worship at riverside/coastal shrines
olokun.cadence: regular and at the Igue/Olokun festivals (Benin)
olokun.notes: Priestesses (ohen) tend altars holding brass figures, coral beads, chalk and water-pots; in Benin the Olokun cult of wealth and fertility is among the most prominent, its shrines built near rivers and the lagoon.

sources.reference: Ben-Amos, The Art of Benin (1980)

oya.name: Egungun masquerade and Oya rites
oya.notes: As the only orisa able to command the egungun (ancestral dead), Oya drives the masquerade between the worlds; her devotees dance with flowing cloths and flywhisks imitating her winds, and she is offered at the Niger and at the marketplace.

sources.reference: Gleason, Oya: In Praise of the Goddess (1987)

phoenician_baal_hammon.name: the molk offering at the Tophet
phoenician_baal_hammon.cadence: in fulfilment of vows and in time of crisis
phoenician_baal_hammon.notes: Burnt offerings (the rite called molk) were made to Baal Hammon and Tanit at open-air precincts (tophets); the cremated remains, of infants and of lambs, were buried in urns under stelae. The practice is most fully attested at Carthage from c. 8th–2nd c. BCE.

sources.reference: Lipiński, Dieux et déesses de l'univers phénicien et punique (1995); Stager, on the Carthage tophet

phoenician_astarte.name: temple service of Astarte at Sidon and Tyre
phoenician_astarte.notes: Chief goddess of the Sidonian and Tyrian royal houses; at Sidon she shared a temple with Eshmun, and Sidonian kings and queens (per the Eshmunazar inscription) served as her priests and built her sanctuaries.

sources.reference: Eshmunazar II sarcophagus inscription (KAI 14), Sidon

pawnee_morning_star.name: the Morning Star sacrifice (captive-girl rite)
pawnee_morning_star.cadence: in years when Mars rose as morning star, prompted by a vision
pawnee_morning_star.notes: The Skidi band's most solemn rite: a captive girl, ritually identified with the Evening Star, was raised on a scaffold of sacred woods (figuring the western garden of creation) and sacrificed at dawn so that fertility might be renewed; last performed 1838.

sources.reference: Linton, The Sacrifice to the Morning Star by the Skidi Pawnee (1922); Murie & Dorsey, Ceremonies of the Pawnee (1981)

otomi_otontecuhtli.name: Xócotl Huetzi (the falling of the fruit)
otomi_otontecuhtli.cadence: annual (Nahua month Xócotl Huetzi, c. August)
otomi_otontecuhtli.notes: A tall pole figuring a tree was raised bearing an amaranth-dough image of Otontecuhtli/Xócotl at its top; after fire-rites for the dead, youths competed to climb the pole and seize the image. The festival joined the harvest of fruit to the cult of fire and the dead.

sources.reference: Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 2 (Anderson & Dibble trans.); López Austin, on Xocotl Huetzi

attributes.name: the sky itself, and the lightning
attributes.notes: Soko denotes both the high god and the sky; he is closely associated with rain and lightning rather than imaged anthropomorphically.

sources.reference: Nadel, Nupe Religion (1954)

attributes.name: the creator represented riding a horse
attributes.notes: Imra was depicted as a rider; his great wooden temple and idol were the chief sanctuary of the Kafirs.

sources.reference: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Nuristan'

attributes.name: carved wooden effigy in a small shrine, with a round face and white-stone eyes
attributes.notes: Cognate Kalash Dizane idols had a round face with white stones for eyes and a quartz mouth; Disani's shrine above Kamdesh was a small carved house with her effigy in the doorway.

sources.reference: Robertson, The Kafirs of the Hindu-Kush (1896)

sacredAnimals.name: the goat (offered at the birth of a son)

sources.reference: Robertson, The Kafirs of the Hindu-Kush (1896)

attributes.name: wooden effigy and shrine hung with the spoils and arms of war
attributes.notes: The popular war-god of the Bashgal; his shrine and image were the focus of the most active Siah-Posh cult.

sources.reference: Robertson, The Kafirs of the Hindu-Kush (1896)

sacredAnimals.name: the giant land snail (igbin), his preferred boneless offering

sources.reference: Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief (1962)

attributes.name: the colour white — white cloth, white chalk (efun), white beads
attributes.notes: All of Obatala's regalia and offerings are white, signifying purity; palm wine is taboo to him.

sources.reference: Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief (1962)

sacredAnimals.name: the dog (his sacrificial animal and companion)

sources.reference: Barnes (ed.), Africa's Ogun (1997)
Barnes (ed.), Africa's Ogun (1997)

attributes.name: iron implements — cutlass, hoe and other forged tools
attributes.notes: Iron and its implements are Ogun's defining attribute and the medium of oaths sworn in his name.

sources.reference: Barnes (ed.), Africa's Ogun (1997)

attributes.name: brass and gold — fans, bracelets and the brass bell (aaja)
attributes.notes: Brass (ide) is Oshun's sacred metal; honey, the mirror and the colour yellow/amber are her tokens.

sources.reference: Badejo, Òṣun Sèègèsí (1996)

sacredAnimals.name: the water buffalo (her avatar)
sacredAnimals.notes: Oya alone among the orisa rises out of the buffalo and returns to it at will.

sources.reference: Gleason, Oya: In Praise of the Goddess (1987)

attributes.name: the flywhisk (iruke), with lightning and the sword
attributes.notes: She is figured by the horsetail/buffalo-tail whisk, the sword, lightning and the whirlwind.

sources.reference: Gleason, Oya: In Praise of the Goddess (1987)

attributes.name: coral and the wealth of the deep — beads, brass figures, water-pots
attributes.notes: Olokun's altars are heaped with coral, glass beads and brass; in Benin court art the divine king's legs are figured as mudfish, linking the Oba to the ocean god.

sources.reference: Ben-Amos, The Art of Benin (1980)

sacredAnimals.name: the mudfish (creature of the watery threshold)

attributes.name: the iron staff crowned with a single bird above a ring of sixteen birds
attributes.notes: The herbalist's wrought-iron staff (opa Osanyin), surmounted by a great bird, is the signature emblem of his medicine.

sources.reference: Thompson, Flash of the Spirit (1983)

attributes.name: the butterfly device (papalotl) on the breast
attributes.notes: His mantled image bears a butterfly insignia, an old fire-and-soul emblem; the festival image was modelled in amaranth dough atop the Xocotl pole.

sources.reference: Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Books 1–2 (Anderson & Dibble trans.)

attributes.name: the warrior painted red, bearing fire and the war-club
attributes.notes: Identified with Mars; in the sacrifice the male principle of the east arrayed in red.
